newsitem.title: FRANCE: French smokers fume over railway station ruling.
newsitem.headline: French smokers fume over railway station ruling.

text.p: French smokers were fuming on Wednesday over the country's first court decision to order a crackdown on tobacco use in public places under a theoretically tough, but virtually unenforced, 1991 law.

"The law was intended to help smokers and non-smokers get along together. If they want to use it to ban smoking altogether in some places, they should revise it," grumbled one Parisian smoker who pleaded anonymity.
A civil court in Lyon ruled on Tuesday that the state-owned SNCF railways had failed adequately to enforce the anti-smoking law in the central French city's Part-Dieu train station.
It fined the SNCF 10,000 francs ($1,818) plus 1,000 francs ($182) a day until adequate enforcement measures were in place.

Officials of the League against Smoking in Public and the National Committee Against Smoking, which brought the complaint, vowed to bring similar actions against other railway stations and rejoiced over their rare victory in a country where smokers' interests generally reign supreme.

A spokesman said the SNCF was weighing an appeal but in the meantime planned to take steps in stations across the country bolstering enforcement of the so-called Evin law, which took effect in November 1991.
"We are extremely sensitive about smoking in our stations, and we are planning measures to assure we are in compliance with the law," an SNCF spokesman said.
The spokesman said an announcement was expected later in the day both on an appeal and on the measures to be taken.
Managers of the Part-Dieu station had posted small no-smoking stickers at entryways and considered their duty done.
But the stickers were "pathetic" and the ban widely breached, according to the Lyon civil law court.
It ordered the SNCF to post bigger and more legible posters throughout the building and also to set aside clearly marked smoking as well as no-smoking zones.
